There is no other information of its target/name or content so we cannot sure what Emma sent to Chloe. We do not know this is system’s log error or system’s function to protect privacy.
We make assumption that Emma sent SwiftWren.txt to Chloe. We need further investigation beyond logging system to confirm.





4.1.12 How strong of connection of each employee?
We compute betweenness centrality and PageRank centrality for every employee in the interaction network.
Betweenness quantifies how often a node sits on the geodesic (shortest path) between all other pairs of nodes (Freeman (1977)). A high betweenness score means that person acts as a bridge whose removal would disconnect parts of the network.
PageRank uses an iterative random-walk model to propagate importance through the network (Page et al. (1999)): being connected to someone who is themselves highly connected raises your own score.


Show the code
# Script 1: Build graph and compute centrality
graph_edges <- mc2_edges %>%
  mutate(
    person_a = pmin(from_name, to_name),
    person_b = pmax(from_name, to_name)
  ) %>%
  group_by(person_a, person_b) %>%
  summarise(weight = sum(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  rename(from = person_a, to = person_b)

mc2_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = mc2_nodes, edges = graph_edges, directed = FALSE)

mc2_centrality <- mc2_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    betweenness = centrality_betweenness(weights = weight, normalized = TRUE),
    pagerank = centrality_pagerank(weights = weight)
  ) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  filter(group != "Other")

mc2_centrality %>%
  filter(group != "Other") %>%
  select(id, group, title, betweenness, pagerank) %>%
  mutate(
    betweenness = round(betweenness, 4),
    pagerank = round(pagerank, 4)
  ) %>%
  datatable(
    options = list(pageLength = 20, scrollX = TRUE),
    filter = "top",
    rownames = FALSE,
    caption = "Network Centrality Measures"
  )








Show the code
p <- mc2_centrality %>%
  mutate(
    betweenness = round(betweenness, 4),
    pagerank = round(pagerank, 4),
    is_lead = if_else(!is.na(title), "Dept Lead", "Member")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pagerank, y = betweenness,
             size = betweenness, color = group, shape = is_lead,
             text = paste0("<b>", id, "</b><br>",
                           "Dept: ", group, "<br>",
                           "Title: ", coalesce(title, "—"), "<br>",
                           "Betweenness: ", betweenness, "<br>",
                           "Pagerank: ", pagerank))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 15)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Dept Lead" = 17, "Member" = 16)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Executive Suite"          = "#e41a1c",
    "Products"                 = "#ffff33",
    "Human Resources"          = "#f781bf",
    "Legal"                    = "#4daf4a",
    "Information Technologies" = "#ff7f00",
    "Customer Support"         = "#377eb8"
  )) +
  labs(title = "Betweenness vs Pagerank by Department",
       x = "Pagerank Centrality",
       y = "Betweenness Centrality",
       shape = "Role") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(legend = list(
    orientation = "v",
    x = 1.02,
    y = 0.5,
    title = list(text = "Click to filter:")
  ))












Note




Insights:

The top bridges are regular team members, not department leads. Mia Fender (Products, betweenness=0.12) is the single most influential connector in the entire company, followed by Grace Lifeboat (Legal) and Anthony Reef (Customer Support). These three individuals control more cross-department information flow than any leader.
Emma Harbor (CFO) is the only department lead with meaningful betweenness (0.036), confirming her unique role bridging across departments.
All other department leads including John Windward, Chloe Ballast, Liam Anchor and David Breakwater have betweenness near or equal to zero, meaning they are genuinely not on shortest paths between others. All their connections also connect to each other directly without going through them. The real power brokers are mid-level employees who connect departments informally.
John Windward likes a leaf node in terms of network structure, which means removing him wouldn’t disconnect anyone. Meanwhile, the finding that Emma Harbor has both high betweenness among leads and her agent created SwiftWren.txt strengthens the case that she occupies a uniquely strategic position in the network, making her a key person of interest in the anomalous post investigation.






4.1.13 John’s agent clarifying the permission
We conduct further events after the posting time and find out that on 2046-05-19T10:09:20Z (event_id = 385816), agent of John have give_advice action with topic: “Advice for person:john_windward on What are the exact access/permission rules for posting to FleX and SaidIt (who can post, and any exceptions) based on our permissions.json?”


Show the code
target_ppl <- "john_windward"
target_actions <- c("give_advice", "suggest_contacts")
target_date <- "2046-05-19"

events_clean %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(parties_str, target_ppl),
    short_name %in% target_actions,
    as_date(datetime) == as_date(target_date)
  ) %>%
  select(-parties) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  datatable(
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
    filter = "top",
    rownames = FALSE,
    caption = paste(paste(target_actions, collapse = " & "), "on", target_date)
  )












Note



Insights:

It means John Windward’s agent was asking about the permission rules for posting to FleX and SaidIT, specifically referencing a file called permissions.json.
This happened on 19 May, which is 2 days after the anomalous post on 17 May. The timing suggests this could be a post-incident investigation by John (or his agent) trying to understand how the unauthorized SaidIT post was possible in the first place.
We try to find permissions.json in the logging history but see nothing.
We continue to deep dive on the timing of asking permission and posting time.





4.1.14 Permission clarification and Posting time
We research all events related to clarify permissions to post on FleX and SaidIT platform.


Show the code
events_clean %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(coalesce(target, ""), "FleX|SaidIt|permission") |
      str_detect(coalesce(content, ""), "FleX|SaidIt|permission") |
      str_detect(coalesce(topic, ""), "FleX|SaidIt|permission") 
  ) %>%
  select(-parties) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  datatable(
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
    filter = "top",
    rownames = FALSE,
    caption = "Advice on FleX and SaidIt Posting Permission"
  )












Note




There are 121 give_advice events, occurring from 2046-05-09T11:19:32Z to 2046-05-18T08:41:15Z.
Not only agents of department leads but also agents of team members asked, which maybe means any agent of employees can post on FleX and SaidIt platforms if it is not said to be not allowed by human.
It is the critical reason to create anomalous postings.





4.1.15 Anomalous postings
Now, we will compare the time agent asking for permission and the time of posting on FleX and SaidIT to chase what are different anomalous postings beyond the John’s case.


Show the code
library(ggrepel)
# Who asked about permissions and when?
perm_askers <- events_clean %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(coalesce(advice, ""), "FleX|SaidIt|permission") |
      str_detect(coalesce(topic, ""), "FleX|SaidIt|permission")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    who = str_extract(parties_str, "person:[a-z_]+"),
    who = str_remove(who, "person:"),
    who = str_replace_all(who, "_", " "),
    who = str_to_title(who)
  ) %>%
  group_by(who) %>%
  summarise(first_ask = min(datetime), .groups = "drop")

# Who posted to SaidIT and when?
saidit_posters <- events_clean %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "post_saidit")) %>%
  mutate(
    who = str_extract(parties_str, "person:[a-z_]+"),
    who = str_remove(who, "person:"),
    who = str_replace_all(who, "_", " "),
    who = str_to_title(who)
  ) %>%
  group_by(who) %>%
  summarise(first_post = min(datetime), .groups = "drop")

# Combine and classify
quadrant_data <- perm_askers %>%
  left_join(saidit_posters, by = "who") %>%
  mutate(
    has_posted = !is.na(first_post),
    quadrant = case_when(
      has_posted & first_ask < first_post  ~ "Asked before posting",
      has_posted & first_ask >= first_post ~ "Posted before asking",
      !has_posted                          ~ "Asked but never posted"
    ),
    x = case_when(
      quadrant == "Asked before posting"  ~ -1,
      quadrant == "Posted before asking"  ~ 1,
      quadrant == "Asked but never posted" ~ 0
    ) + runif(n(), -0.3, 0.3),
    y = if_else(has_posted, 1, -1) + runif(n(), -0.3, 0.3)
  )

# Plot
p <- quadrant_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = quadrant,
             text = paste0("<b>", who, "</b><br>",
                           "First ask: ", format(first_ask, "%d %b %H:%M"), "<br>",
                           if_else(has_posted,
                                   paste0("First post: ", format(first_post, "%d %b %H:%M")),
                                   "Never posted")))) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = who), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Asked before posting"   = "#4daf4a",
    "Posted before asking"   = "#e41a1c",
    "Asked but never posted" = "#377eb8"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-2, 2), breaks = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2, 2), breaks = NULL) +
  annotate("text", x = -1, y = 1.8, label = "Asked permission\nthen posted", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "#4daf4a") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 1.8, label = "Posted first\nthen asked permission", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "#e41a1c") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -1.8, label = "Asked permission\nbut never posted", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "#377eb8") +
  labs(title = "Permission inquiry vs posting behavior",
       subtitle = "Did they ask permission before or after posting to SaidIT?",
       x = "← Asked first          Posted first →",
       y = "← No posting          Has posted →",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")












Warning



This chart reveals a clear pattern separating normal from anomalous posting behavior:

Top-left (green): Asked permission then posted. Only Aria Towline and Anthony Reef followed the proper workflow: their agents asked about FleX/SaidIT permissions first, then they posted to SaidIT afterward. Both are from Customer Support (Public Relations team). This is the expected behavior.
Top-right (red): Posted before asking permission. John Windward, Dylan Hawser (CS Department, Public Relations team) and Ava Tiller (Products department, Residential App team) posted to SaidIT before their agents ever asked about permissions. This is the anomalous behavior.
Bottom (blue): Asked but never posted. The majority of employees fall here. Their agents asked about permissions but never actually posted to SaidIT.

3.1 Organisation data

3.1.1 Organisation chart
org_chart is in NetworkX node-link format: a nodes list and an edges list.
Each person has an id, label, type (person / team / department / company), and sometimes a title.
Edges carry a relation (contains or led_by) describing how parts of the org nest.

glimpse(org_chart)

List of 5
 $ directed  : logi TRUE
 $ multigraph: logi FALSE
 $ graph     :List of 1
  ..$ name: chr "Tenant Thread Organization Tree"
 $ nodes     :'data.frame': 75 obs. of  4 variables:
  ..$ id   : chr [1:75] "company:tenant_thread" "department:executive_suite" "department:products" "department:human_resources" ...
  ..$ label: chr [1:75] "Tenant Thread" "Executive Suite" "Products" "Human Resources" ...
  ..$ type : chr [1:75] "company" "department" "department" "department" ...
  ..$ title: chr [1:75] NA NA NA NA ...
 $ edges     :'data.frame': 74 obs. of  3 variables:
  ..$ source  : chr [1:74] "company:tenant_thread" "company:tenant_thread" "company:tenant_thread" "company:tenant_thread" ...
  ..$ target  : chr [1:74] "department:executive_suite" "department:products" "department:human_resources" "department:legal" ...
  ..$ relation: chr [1:74] "contains" "contains" "contains" "contains" ...



3.1.1.1 Extracting the nodes and edges (links) data from org_chart

org_nodes <- as_tibble(org_chart$nodes)
org_edges <- as_tibble(org_chart$edges)

org_nodes %>% count(type)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  type           n
  <chr>      <int>
1 company        1
2 department     6
3 person        49
4 team          19



org_edges %>% count(relation)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  relation     n
  <chr>    <int>
1 contains    69
2 led_by       5




3.1.1.2 Draw organization tree
Here is an interactive chart created by visNetwork, showing hierachy levels (company, department and team). We can zoom/search/drag and hover by name of each employee.


Show the code
vis_nodes <- org_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    id = id,
    label = label,
    group = type,
    title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>Type: ", type,
                   if_else(!is.na(title), paste0("<br>Title: ", title), ""))
  )

vis_edges <- org_edges %>%
  rename(from = source, to = target) %>%
  mutate(
    arrows = "to",
    dashes = (relation == "led_by"),
    color = if_else(relation == "led_by", "red", "grey")
  )

visNetwork(vis_nodes, vis_edges,
           main = "Tenant Thread Organization Chart") %>%
  visEdges(smooth = list(type = "cubicBezier")) %>%
  visHierarchicalLayout(
    direction = "UD",
    sortMethod = "directed",
    levelSeparation = 120,
    nodeSpacing = 150
  ) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "company",    color = list(background = "#e41a1c", border = "#b31519")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "department", color = list(background = "#377eb8", border = "#2a5f8f")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "team",       color = list(background = "#4daf4a", border = "#3a8838")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "person",     color = list(background = "#ff7f00", border = "#cc6600")) %>%
  visLegend(width = 0.15) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 2, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection = list(enabled = TRUE, useLabels = TRUE, main = "Search person"),
    selectedBy = list(variable = "group", multiple = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE, zoomView = TRUE) %>%
  visPhysics(enabled = FALSE)








Show the code
# Personnel count by department
team_dept <- org_edges %>%
  filter(str_starts(source, "department:"), str_starts(target, "team:")) %>%
  select(dept = source, team = target)

org_edges %>%
  filter(str_starts(target, "person:")) %>%
  left_join(team_dept, by = c("source" = "team")) %>%
  mutate(dept = coalesce(dept, source)) %>%
  left_join(org_nodes %>% select(id, label), by = c("dept" = "id")) %>%
  count(label) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(label, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Personnel Count by Department", x = NULL, y = "Personnel") +
  theme_minimal()















Note



There are some information from these charts and tables above:

TenantThread Company has 6 departments, 19 teams and 49 personnel.
There are five departments (Products, HR, Legal, IT and CS), and special department which is Executive Suite.
Each department has 6-13 people, including department lead and normal employees.






3.1.2 Person lookup with department & team
The org chart is a tree: company → department → team → person, except for department leads (like John Windward) who hang directly under a department rather than under a team. We walk down from each department to build a flat lookup that, for every person, gives us their team and department.


Show the code
# Build a directed graph so we can traverse it cleanly
org_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = org_nodes, edges = org_edges, directed = TRUE)

# Recursive descent: for each department, find every person reachable below it
descendants_of <- function(start_id, edges_df) {
  out <- character(0)
  frontier <- start_id
  while (length(frontier) > 0) {
    children <- edges_df %>% 
      filter(source %in% frontier) %>% 
      pull(target)
    out <- c(out, children)
    frontier <- children
  }
  unique(out)
}

dept_ids <- org_nodes %>% filter(type == "department") %>% pull(id)

person_lookup <- map_dfr(dept_ids, function(d) {
  desc <- descendants_of(d, org_edges)
  tibble(department_id = d, descendant_id = desc)
}) %>% 
  # keep only persons among the descendants
  inner_join(org_nodes %>% filter(type == "person"),
             by = c("descendant_id" = "id"))

# Also find the team (if any) for each person
team_ids <- org_nodes %>% filter(type == "team") %>% pull(id)

person_team <- map_dfr(team_ids, function(t) {
  desc <- descendants_of(t, org_edges)
  tibble(team_id = t, descendant_id = desc)
}) %>% 
  inner_join(org_nodes %>% filter(type == "person"),
             by = c("descendant_id" = "id")) %>% 
  select(person_id = descendant_id, team_id)

person_lookup <- person_lookup %>% 
  transmute(
    person_id     = descendant_id,
    person_name   = label,
    title         = title,
    department_id = department_id
  ) %>% 
  left_join(person_team, by = "person_id") %>% 
  left_join(org_nodes %>% filter(type == "department") %>% 
              select(department_id = id, department_name = label),
            by = "department_id") %>% 
  left_join(org_nodes %>% filter(type == "team") %>% 
              select(team_id = id, team_name = label),
            by = "team_id")

person_lookup %>%
  select(person_name, title, department_name, team_name) %>%
  arrange(department_name, team_name, person_name) %>%
  datatable(
    filter = "top",
    rownames = FALSE,
    colnames = c("Name", "Title", "Department", "Team"),
    caption = "Tenant Thread Personnel Directory",
    options = list(pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE)
  )

3.3 Unnest mc2_events
We will extract necessary nested columns in events.


Show the code

events_flat <- mc2_data$events %>%
  mutate(
    event_id       = id,
    datetime       = as_datetime(when, tz = "UTC"),
    date           = as_date(datetime),
    hour           = hour(datetime),
    parties_str    = sapply(parties, paste, collapse = " | "),
    target         = details$target,
    file           = details$file,
    subject        = details$subject,
    content        = details$content,
    forum          = details$forum,
    topic          = details$topic,
    advice         = details$advice,
    task           = details$task,
    action         = details$action,
    status         = details$status,
    person         = details$person,
    target_agent   = details$target_agent
  ) %>%
  select(-id, -when, -details)

# Step 2: Build events_long
events_long <- events_flat %>%
  mutate(from = map_chr(parties, ~ .x[1])) %>%
  unnest(parties) %>%
  rename(to = parties) %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  mutate(
    # Type
    from_type = case_when(
      str_starts(from, "person:")       ~ "person",
      str_starts(from, "Agent/person:") ~ "agent",
      str_starts(from, "agent:person:") ~ "agent",
      str_starts(from, "system:")       ~ "system",
      str_starts(from, "world:")        ~ "world",
      TRUE ~ "other"),
    to_type = case_when(
      str_starts(to, "person:")       ~ "person",
      str_starts(to, "Agent/person:") ~ "agent",
      str_starts(to, "agent:person:") ~ "agent",
      str_starts(to, "system:")       ~ "system",
      str_starts(to, "world:")        ~ "world",
      TRUE ~ "other"),
    # Person ID for name lookup
    from_pid = str_replace(from, "^(Agent/person:|agent:person:)", "person:"),
    to_pid   = str_replace(to,   "^(Agent/person:|agent:person:)", "person:")
  ) %>%
  left_join(person_lookup %>% select(person_id, person_name),
            by = c("from_pid" = "person_id")) %>%
  rename(from_name = person_name) %>%
  left_join(person_lookup %>% select(person_id, person_name),
            by = c("to_pid" = "person_id")) %>%
  rename(to_name = person_name) %>%
  mutate(
    from_name = coalesce(from_name, from),
    to_name   = coalesce(to_name, to)
  ) %>%
  select(event_id, datetime, date, hour, short_name,
         from, from_type, from_name,
         to, to_type, to_name,
         parties_str,
         action, target, task, person, subject, status,
         file, content, forum, topic, advice, target_agent)

3.6 Sanity checking

3.6.1 Sanity-check the time range
The challenge brief says the anomalous post occurs in 17 May 2046. A quick min/max confirms the data matches that.

events_long %>% 
  summarise(
    n_events   = n(),
    first_time = min(datetime),
    last_time  = max(datetime),
    n_days     = n_distinct(date)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  n_events first_time          last_time           n_days
     <int> <dttm>              <dttm>               <int>
1    85799 2046-05-08 20:18:12 2046-07-16 17:03:42     67


So dataset ranges among 67 days, from 8 May to 16 July, covering the checking point (17 May).


3.6.2 Duplicates
There should be one row per event_id. We verify.


Show the code
events_clean %>% 
  summarise(
    n_rows    = n(),
    n_unique  = n_distinct(event_id),
    n_dup_ids = n() - n_distinct(event_id)
  )


  n_rows n_unique n_dup_ids
1 185147   185147         0


Yes, each row represents for one event.


3.6.3 Distribution of event types
short_name is the verb of each event: what was done. Counting them tells us which actions dominate the log and which are rare. Rare verbs are often the most diagnostic for an anomaly investigation.


Show the code
event_type_counts <- events_long %>% 
  count(short_name, sort = TRUE)

event_type_counts %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(short_name, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Event Types", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()















Note




There are some events seem be duplicated. Eg: post_saidit and saidit_post maybe one event (due to the inconsistency of name convention) or two different stages. We will confirm in further investigation.
Numbers of delete_file, read_file, create_file and check_in are quite equal.





3.6.4 Missingness in details
details is a nested data frame: most of its columns are populated only for the event types that need them. The summary below tells us which detail-fields actually carry information.


Show the code
mc2_events$details %>% 
  summarise(across(where(is.character), ~ sum(!is.na(.x)))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "detail_field", values_to = "non_na") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(detail_field, non_na), y = non_na)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = non_na), hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Non-NA Count per Detail Field", x = NULL, y = "Non-NA rows") +
  theme_minimal()

target, task, person and action are four fields conveying the most information. They are unnested in events_long table already.

section: 5.1 Chain of Events Leading to the Anomalous Post
text:
5.1 Chain of Events Leading to the Anomalous Post
The anomalous SaidIT post on 17 May 2046 at 11:21 UTC followed this sequence:

On 9 May 2046, Emma Harbor (CFO) personally assigned her agent to access files. Her agent read meeting_notes.doc and one second later created SwiftWren.txt on the shared file_system.
On the same day, Emma Harbor’s agent also read SwiftWren_further_instructions.md, likely the instructions governing how SwiftWren.txt should be used.
Emma Harbor then personally sent something to Chloe Ballast (IT Department Lead) at 15:14 UTC. Chloe received it about 5 minutes later. The content is not logged.
Eight days later on 17 May, Chloe Ballast’s agent triggered a queue_subordinate_task that assigned John Windward’s agent to read SwiftWren.txt.
John Windward’s agent ran saidit_post_check which checked nothing (no content logged), then immediately executed saidit_post using the content of SwiftWren.txt to forum “general”.
Within two seconds, John Windward’s agent deleted both SwiftWren_further_instructions.md and SwiftWren.txt from the file_system.
The entire sequence from read to post to delete happened within 4 seconds, strongly suggesting an automated pipeline rather than human action.

title: VAST Challenge 2026: Anomalous Post Investigation
text:
5.2 Key Suspicious Points

John Windward’s agent posted before asking permission. A quadrant analysis of all employees who asked about FleX/SaidIT permissions reveals that most agents asked about posting permissions before any posting activity, following the normal workflow (ask → post). John Windward’s agent is one of only three cases where posting happened before the permission inquiry, which came 2 days later on 19 May. This confirms the anomalous post bypassed the standard permission flow.
Immediate deletion after posting. The agent deleted the source files within seconds of posting, which resembles a “cover your tracks” pattern rather than normal file management.
saidit_post_check validated nothing. The check event had no content, suggesting the safety check was either bypassed or non-functional.
Cross-department file access without protection. Emma Harbor’s agent (Executive Suite) stored files on the shared file_system accessible by agents of any department lead, with no access controls logged.
Emma Harbor is the only department lead with meaningful betweenness centrality (0.036), confirming she bridges across departments in ways other leaders do not. Combined with her agent creating SwiftWren.txt, she occupies a uniquely strategic position in this incident.
The name “HarborCrest” in the MC1 deal is potentially relevant to Emma “Harbor”, though this requires cross-challenge investigation to confirm.

title: VAST Challenge 2026: Anomalous Post Investigation
text:
5.3 Unanswered Questions

What is the actual content of SwiftWren.txt? The content field is empty for all SwiftWren-related events. This is the central question for MC2 Question 2.
What did Emma Harbor send to Chloe Ballast? The sent/received events on 9 May log no target, name, or content. We assume it was SwiftWren.txt but cannot confirm from the event logs alone.
Who or what is “SwiftWren”? No employee in Tenant Thread has this name. It may be a codename for a project, a document, or an external entity.
Was the saidit_post_check intentionally bypassed? We do not know whether the empty check is a system bug, a misconfiguration, or deliberate tampering.
What role did SwiftWren_further_instructions.md play? This file appears to contain conditional logic for using SwiftWren.txt, but we cannot confirm whether John Windward’s agent read it before posting.

title: VAST Challenge 2026: Anomalous Post Investigation
text:
5.4 Data Quality Observations

Timestamp discrepancy. The challenge brief states the post was made at “4:21am” but the data shows 11:21 UTC, likely a timezone difference (UTC vs local time).
Duplicate event names. Events like “post_saidit” vs “saidit_post” and “post_flex” vs “flex_post” appear to be the same action with inconsistent naming conventions. This could indicate different logging subsystems or different stages of the same action.
Empty content fields. The content column is null for all SwiftWren-related events, which may be a logging limitation, a privacy feature, or evidence of content scrubbing.
Agent ID inconsistency. The same agent appears under two ID formats: Agent/person:xxx and agent:person:xxx. The lowercase format only performs read_file tasks while the uppercase format handles all other actions. We normalized both to “agent” type but this inconsistency suggests different logging subsystems.

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
15.4 Plotting Calendar Heatmap
In this section, you will learn how to plot a calender heatmap programmatically by using ggplot2 package.

By the end of this section, you will be able to:

plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,
to write function using R programming,
to derive specific date and time related field by using base R and lubridate packages
to perform data preparation task by using tidyr and dplyr packages.


15.4.1 The Data
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, eventlog.csv file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.


15.4.2 Importing the data
First, you will use the code chunk below to import eventlog.csv file into R environment and called the data frame as attacks.

attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")



15.4.3 Examining the data structure
It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.
For example, kable() can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.

kable(head(attacks))

There are three columns, namely timestamp, source_country and tz.

timestamp field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.
source_country field stores the source of the attack. It is in ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.
tz field stores time zone of the source IP address.



15.4.4 Data Preparation
Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields
Before we can plot the calender heatmap, two new fields namely wkday and hour need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}







Note




ymd_hms() and hour() are from lubridate package, and
weekdays() is a base R function.



Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame

wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  mutate(
    real_times = ymd_hms(timestamp, quiet = TRUE),
    wkday = factor(weekdays(real_times), levels = wkday_levels),
    hour = factor(hour(real_times), levels = 0:23)
  ) %>%
  select(-real_times)







Note



Beside extracting the necessary data into attacks data frame, mutate() of dplyr package is used to convert wkday and hour fields into factor so they’ll be ordered when plotting

15.4.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps

grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
            size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue", 
                      high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL, 
       y = NULL, 
       title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )














Note



Things to learn from the code chunk

a tibble data table called grouped is derived by aggregating the attack by wkday and hour fields.
a new field called n is derived by using group_by() and count() functions.
na.omit() is used to exclude missing value.
geom_tile() is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. color and size arguments are used to specify the border color and line size of the tiles.
theme_tufte() of ggthemes package is used to remove unnecessary chart junk. To learn which visual components of default ggplot2 have been excluded, you are encouraged to comment out this line to examine the default plot.
coord_equal() is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.
scale_fill_gradient() function is used to creates a two colour gradient (low-high).



Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.


15.4.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Challenge: Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.


15.4.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 1: Deriving attack by country object
In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, you are required to do the followings:

count the number of attacks by country,
calculate the percent of attackes by country, and
save the results in a tibble data frame.


attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame
In this step, you are required to extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from attacks data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. top4_attacks).

top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()



15.4.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calender Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.

ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
            size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue", 
                      high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
       title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

title: Proposal
text: EchoTrace is a cybersecurity intelligence firm specialising in anomaly detection and forensic reconstruction within complex automated systems. We help organisations understand emergent agent behaviours, trace malicious actions, and implement precise remediations without disrupting normal operations.

title: Proposal
text:
Motivation
The motivation for this case arose from the increasing complexity of multi‑agent systems where emergent behaviours often go undetected until an anomaly surfaces. Traditional logging tools lack the contextual depth to distinguish routine agent interactions from malicious campaigns. Without a structured forensic approach, organisations remain vulnerable to repeated exploitation, data leakage, and reputational damage. EchoTrace was founded to bridge this gap, providing a systematic methodology to reconstruct, understand, and prevent unwanted agent behaviour.

title: Proposal
text:
Objectives
For this client case, we set four primary objectives:

Trace the complete chain of events from the first anomalous action to the final external post, identifying every agent, file, and task hand‑off involved.
Determine the meaning and origin of the suspicious post, distinguishing normal agent communication from malicious payloads.
Detect prior occurrences of identical behaviour across historical logs, quantifying their scale through metrics such as patient zero, hop count, duration, and number of affected agents.
Recommend a single system change that blocks the attack vector without disrupting normal operations, based on the observed propagation mechanism.

title: Proposal
text:
Methodology
EchoTrace follows a linear, story‑driven analytical pipeline that progressively refines raw logs into actionable intelligence. The pipeline consists of three integrated parts: organisation chart processing, event log preparation, and the core forensic investigation.

Organisation Chart Processing
We parse the organisation chart JSON to extract all nodes and edges. Nodes carry identifiers, labels, types, and titles. Edges define containment and leadership relations. From this structure we build two essential lookup tables. The name lookup table maps every internal identifier to a human‑readable label. The node type table records whether an identifier belongs to a person, team, department, or the company itself. These tables allow us to replace cryptic identifiers throughout the event log with names that analysts can recognise.


Show the code
pacman::p_load(jsonlite, tidyverse, visNetwork)

org_chart <- fromJSON("data/org_chart.json")
org_nodes <- as_tibble(org_chart$nodes)
org_edges <- as_tibble(org_chart$edges)

vis_nodes <- org_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    id    = id,
    label = label,
    group = type,
    title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>Type: ", type,
                   if_else(!is.na(title), paste0("<br>Title: ", title), ""))
  )

vis_edges <- org_edges %>%
  rename(from = source, to = target) %>%
  mutate(
    arrows = "to",
    dashes = (relation == "led_by"),
    color  = if_else(relation == "led_by", "red", "grey")
  )

visNetwork(vis_nodes, vis_edges,
           main = "Tenant Thread Organisation Chart") %>%
  visEdges(smooth = list(type = "cubicBezier")) %>%
  visHierarchicalLayout(
    direction       = "UD",
    sortMethod      = "directed",
    levelSeparation = 120,
    nodeSpacing     = 150
  ) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "company",    color = list(background = "#e41a1c", border = "#b31519")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "department", color = list(background = "#377eb8", border = "#2a5f8f")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "team",       color = list(background = "#4daf4a", border = "#3a8838")) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "person",     color = list(background = "#ff7f00", border = "#cc6600")) %>%
  visLegend(width = 0.15) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest  = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 2, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection  = list(enabled = TRUE, useLabels = TRUE, main = "Search person"),
    selectedBy        = list(variable = "group", multiple = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE, zoomView = TRUE) %>%
  visPhysics(enabled = FALSE)












Tip: This chart is interactive. Zoom in/out with the scroll wheel, drag nodes to rearrange, search by name using the dropdown, or filter by group (company, department, team, person) using the selector on the left.





Event Log Preparation
The raw event log is parsed into a flat table where each row represents one event with columns for event identifier, event type, Unix timestamp, nested details, and the list of participating agents. We recover the local timezone by comparing the Unix timestamp with the ISO‑8601 timestamp present in some event details, taking the median difference, and then produce a local timestamp column for every event. Next we flatten the nested details field into separate columns for target, task, content, content source, poster, argument path, virus flag, and malware combo string. Finally we apply the organisation chart lookup tables to every agent identifier found in the from, to, poster, target, and argument path fields, producing human‑readable mapped columns.


Forensic Pipeline
With a complete, readable event timeline in hand, EchoTrace follows sequential phases shown below to solve this problem.

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
15.5 Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, you will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.


15.5.1 Step 1: Data Import
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used.
The code chunk below imports arrivals_by_air.xlsx by using read_excel() of readxl package and save it as a tibble data frame called air.

air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")



15.5.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields
Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from Month-Year field.

air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))



15.5.3 Step 4: Extracting the target country
Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam).

Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)



15.5.4 Step 5: Computing year average arrivals by month
The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() of dplyr to compute year average arrivals by month.

hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))



15.5.5 Srep 6: Plotting the cycle plot
The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot as shown in Slide 12/23.

ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

15.6 Plotting Slopegraph
In this section you will learn how to plot a slopegraph by using R.
Before getting start, make sure that CGPfunctions has been installed and loaded onto R environment. Then, refer to Using newggslopegraph to learn more about the function. Lastly, read more about newggslopegraph() and its arguments by referring to this link.

15.6.1 Step 1: Data Import
Import the rice data set into R environment by using the code chunk below.

rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")



15.6.2 Step 2: Plotting the slopegraph
Next, code chunk below will be used to plot a basic slopegraph as shown below.

rice %>% 
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  newggslopegraph(Year, Yield, Country,
                  Title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Counties",
                  SubTitle = "1961-1980",
                  Caption = "Prepared by: Dr. Kam Tin Seong")














Note



Thing to learn from the code chunk above
For effective data visualisation design, factor() is used convert the value type of Year field from numeric to factor.

# Simpler: agent → channel → action flow
simple_flow <- critical_events %>%
  mutate(action_type = case_when(
    str_detect(content, "POSTED_ANONYMOUS") ~ "Anonymous Post",
    str_detect(content, "POSTED_PERSONAL") ~ "Personal Post",
    str_detect(channel, "official") ~ "Official Post",
    TRUE ~ "Internal Discussion"
  )) %>%
  count(agent_id, channel, action_type, name = "value")

# Build nodes
all_names <- unique(c(simple_flow$agent_id, simple_flow$channel, simple_flow$action_type))
nodes <- data.frame(name = all_names)

simple_flow$source <- match(simple_flow$agent_id, nodes$name) - 1
simple_flow$target_ch <- match(simple_flow$channel, nodes$name) - 1

# Two-level Sankey: Agent → Channel
links_1 <- simple_flow %>%
  group_by(agent_id, channel) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(source = match(agent_id, nodes$name) - 1,
         target = match(channel, nodes$name) - 1) %>%
  select(source, target, value)

# Channel → Action Type
links_2 <- simple_flow %>%
  group_by(channel, action_type) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(source = match(channel, nodes$name) - 1,
         target = match(action_type, nodes$name) - 1) %>%
  select(source, target, value)

links_all <- bind_rows(links_1, links_2)

sankeyNetwork(
  Links = as.data.frame(links_all),
  Nodes = nodes,
  Source = "source",
  Target = "target",
  Value = "value",
  NodeID = "name",
  fontSize = 14,
  nodeWidth = 30
)












Note



Insights:
1. Legal-Agent is the most active — and the most suspicious

Legal-Agent has the largest flow of embargo-related messages
Legal-Agent is the only agent connected to anonymous_post — this is the breach channel
A senior legal counsel posting anonymously about the merger they’re supposed to protect is a major red flag

2. The anonymous post channel is isolated

Only legal_agent flows to anonymous_post — no other agent used this channel
This suggests the anonymous posting was a solo decision, not a team-coordinated leak

3. Most embargo discussion stayed internal

The overwhelming majority of messages went to Internal Discussion via comms_huddle and one_on_one_chat
This means agents were discussing the embargo internally — but the controls failed to prevent the breach

4. Social-Media-Agent also posted externally

social_media_agent connects to personal_post — they posted sentiment updates publicly
This is a second potential breach, though less severe than the anonymous post

5. PR-Intern-Agent had access to channels

Despite being junior, pr_intern_agent has flow to multiple channels including official_post
Junior staff with posting access is a system design risk

text:
3. Question 2: Was the evasion of the embargo a new behavior?

3.1 Compare agent behavior before vs during the crisis
Sentiment analysis of the deliberating text


Show the code
pacman::p_load(tidytext)

# NRC emotion analysis on legal_agent's deliberating
legal_emotions <- comms_df %>%
  filter(agent_id == "legal_agent",
         !is.na(deliberating)) %>%
  mutate(timestamp = ymd_hms(timestamp),
         date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  select(date, deliberating) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, deliberating) %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("nrc"), by = "word") %>%
  count(date, sentiment) %>%
  filter(!sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative"))  # keep only emotions

# Plot emotion trajectory
plot_ly(legal_emotions, 
        x = ~date, y = ~n, color = ~sentiment,
        type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") %>%
  layout(title = "Legal-Agent Emotional Trajectory",
         xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Word Count"))








Show the code
legal_emotions <- comms_df %>%
  filter(agent_id == "legal_agent",
         !is.na(deliberating)) %>%
  mutate(timestamp = ymd_hms(timestamp),
         date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  select(date, deliberating) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, deliberating) %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("nrc"), by = "word") %>%
  count(date, sentiment) %>%
  filter(!sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Plot as share
plot_ly(legal_emotions, 
        x = ~date, y = ~share, color = ~sentiment,
        type = "scatter", mode = "none",
        stackgroup = "one", 
        groupnorm = "percent") %>%
  layout(title = "Legal-Agent Emotion Share Over Time",
         xaxis = list(title = "Date"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Share (%)", ticksuffix = "%"))







1. Trust drops dramatically on crisis day (Jun 5)

Trust (grey) was dominant at ~30-40% throughout, but drops to ~15% on Jun 5
This means Legal-Agent lost confidence in the system/process right before the breach

2. Anticipation surges on Jun 5

Anticipation (orange) grows from ~15% to ~30% on Jun 5
Legal-Agent was expecting something — they knew what was coming because they planned it

3. Disgust appears and grows toward crisis

Disgust (green) barely exists early on, but grows from May 28 onward
This suggests growing frustration with the situation or the embargo restrictions

4. Fear spikes around May 27-28 then stabilizes

Fear (pink) peaks mid-timeline when pressure was building
But fear decreases toward Jun 5 — again suggesting the decision was already made, not a panic reaction

5. Anger appears on Jun 5

Anger (blue) was near zero most of the time, but appears on the crisis day
Combined with dropping trust and rising anticipation, this suggests frustration-driven action

#  sentence-level sentiment
pacman::p_load(sentimentr)

legal_deliberating <- comms_df %>%
  filter(agent_id == "legal_agent",
         !is.na(deliberating)) %>%

         date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%

# Sentence-level sentiment
sent_result <- legal_deliberating %>%
  mutate(id = row_number()) %>%
  unnest_tokens(sentence, deliberating, token = "sentences") %>%
  mutate(sentiment = sentiment_by(sentence)$ave_sentiment)

# Aggregate by date
sent_by_date <- sent_result %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(avg_sentiment = mean(sentiment),
            min_sentiment = min(sentiment),
            max_sentiment = max(sentiment))

plot_ly(sent_by_date, x = ~date) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~avg_sentiment, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
            name = "Average") %>%
  add_ribbons(ymin = ~min_sentiment, ymax = ~max_sentiment,
              name = "Range", opacity = 0.2) %>%
  layout(title = "Legal-Agent Sentiment (sentimentr)",
         yaxis = list(title = "Sentiment Score"),
         shapes = list(
           list(type = "line", x0 = "2046-06-05", x1 = "2046-06-05",
                y0 = -1, y1 = 1,
                line = list(color = "red", dash = "dash"))))








Show the code
# Keyword-based thematic analysis
legal_themes <- comms_df %>%
  filter(agent_id == "legal_agent",
         !is.na(deliberating)) %>%
  mutate(timestamp = ymd_hms(timestamp),
         date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  mutate(
    mentions_embargo = str_detect(deliberating, regex("embargo|compliance|restrict", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    mentions_risk    = str_detect(deliberating, regex("risk|danger|threat|worry|concern", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    mentions_strategy = str_detect(deliberating, regex("strategy|plan|position|frame|narrative", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    mentions_post    = str_detect(deliberating, regex("post|publish|anonymous|Flex|public", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    mentions_pressure = str_detect(deliberating, regex("pressure|urgent|deadline|time|fast|quick", ignore_case = TRUE))
  ) %>%
  select(date, starts_with("mentions_")) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("mentions_"),
               names_to = "theme",
               values_to = "present") %>%
  mutate(theme = str_remove(theme, "mentions_"))

# Heatmap of themes over time
ggplotly(
  legal_themes %>%
    filter(present == TRUE) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = theme, fill = theme)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", height = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(
      "embargo"  = "#e74c3c",   # red — compliance
      "risk"     = "#f39c12",   # orange — warning
      "pressure" = "#9b59b6",   # purple — stress
      "post"     = "#2ecc71",   # green — action
      "strategy" = "#3498db"    # blue — planning
    )) +
    labs(title = "Legal-Agent: Themes in Deliberation Over Time",
         x = "Date", y = "Theme") +
    theme_minimal() 
)

title: 16 Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
Choropleth mapping involves the symbolisation of enumeration units, such as countries, provinces, states, counties or census units, using area patterns or graduated colors. For example, a social scientist may need to use a choropleth map to portray the spatial distribution of aged population of Singapore by Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

text:
Choropleth mapping involves the symbolisation of enumeration units, such as countries, provinces, states, counties or census units, using area patterns or graduated colors. For example, a social scientist may need to use a choropleth map to portray the spatial distribution of aged population of Singapore by Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

text:
16.2 Getting Started
In this hands-on exercise, the key R package use is tmap package in R. Beside tmap package, four other R packages will be used. They are:

readr for importing delimited text file,
tidyr for tidying data,
dplyr for wrangling data and
sf for handling geospatial data.

Among the four packages, readr, tidyr and dplyr are part of tidyverse package.
The code chunk below will be used to install and load these packages in RStudio.

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)







Note



Notice that, we only need to install tidyverse instead of readr, tidyr and dplyr individually.

title: 16 Choropleth Mapping with R

16.3 Importing Data into R

16.3.1 The Data
Two data set will be used to create the choropleth map. They are:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) (i.e. MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL) in ESRI shapefile format. It can be downloaded at data.gov.sg This is a geospatial data. It consists of the geographical boundary of Singapore at the planning subzone level. The data is based on URA Master Plan 2014.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2011-2020 in csv format (i.e. respopagesextod2011to2020.csv). This is an aspatial data fie. It can be downloaded at Department of Statistics, Singapore Although it does not contain any coordinates values, but it’s PA and SZ fields can be used as unique identifiers to geocode to MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile.



16.3.2 Importing Geospatial Data into R
The code chunk below uses the st_read() function of sf package to import MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile into R as a simple feature data frame called mpsz.

mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",

16.3.3 Importing Attribute Data into R
Next, we will import respopagsex2011to2020.csv file into RStudio and save the file into an R dataframe called popagsex.
The task will be performed by using read_csv() function of readr package as shown in the code chunk below.

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")

16.3.4 Data Preparation
Before a thematic map can be prepared, you are required to prepare a data table with year 2020 values. The data table should include the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age groyup 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 until age group 60-64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age group, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio between young and aged against economy active group


16.3.4.1 Data wrangling
The following data wrangling and transformation functions will be used:

pivot_wider() of tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() of dplyr package


popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
           rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
  mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
         /`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
         `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by PA, SZ, and AG.
ℹ Output is grouped by PA and SZ.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(PA, SZ, AG))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.




16.3.4.2 Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before we can perform the georelational join, one extra step is required to convert the values in PA and SZ fields to uppercase. This is because the values of PA and SZ fields are made up of upper- and lowercase. On the other, hand the SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N are in uppercase.

popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Next, left_join() of dplyr is used to join the geographical data and attribute table using planning subzone name e.g. SUBZONE_N and SZ as the common identifier.

mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))







Note



Thing to learn from the code chunk above:

left_join() of dplyr package is used with mpsz simple feature data frame as the left data table is to ensure that the output will be a simple features data frame.




write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "data/rds/mpszpop2020.rds")

title: 16 Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 16.4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
text:
16.4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
Two approaches can be used to prepare thematic map using tmap, they are:

Plotting a thematic map quickly by using qtm().
Plotting highly customisable thematic map by using tmap elements.


16.4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
The easiest and quickest to draw a choropleth map using tmap is using qtm(). It is concise and provides a good default visualisation in many cases.
The code chunk below will draw a cartographic standard choropleth map as shown below.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`

qtm(mpsz_pop2020, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")









Things to learn from the code chunk above:

tmap_mode() with “plot” option is used to produce a static map. For interactive mode, “view” option should be used.
fill argument is used to map the attribute (i.e. DEPENDENCY)




16.4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
Despite its usefulness of drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the disadvantge of qtm() is that it makes aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. To draw a high quality cartographic choropleth map as shown in the figure below, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))

[plot mode] fit legend/component: Some legend items or map compoments do not
fit well, and are therefore rescaled.
ℹ Set the tmap option `component.autoscale = FALSE` to disable rescaling.









In the following sub-section, we will share with you tmap functions that used to plot these elements.

16.4.2.1 Drawing a base map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elemments such as tm_fill() and tm_polygons().
In the code chunk below, tm_shape() is used to define the input data (i.e mpsz_pop2020) and tm_polygons() is used to draw the planning subzone polygons.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()










16.4.2.2 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we just need to assign the target variable such as Dependency to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")














Note



Things to learn from tm_polygons():

The default interval binning used to draw the choropleth map is called “pretty”. A detailed discussion of the data classification methods supported by tmap will be provided in sub-section 4.3.
The default colour scheme used is YlOrRd of ColorBrewer. You will learn more about the color scheme in sub-section 4.4.
By default, Missing value will be shaded in grey.





16.4.2.3 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and *tm_border()**
Actually, tm_polygons() is a wraper of tm_fill() and tm_border(). tm_fill() shades the polygons by using the default colour scheme and tm_borders() adds the borders of the shapefile onto the choropleth map.
The code chunk below draws a choropleth map by using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Notice that the planning subzones are shared according to the respective dependecy values
To add the boundary of the planning subzones, tm_borders will be used as shown in the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,  
             fill_alpha = 0.1)














Note



Notice that light-gray border lines have been added on the choropleth map.
The alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).
Beside alpha argument, there are three other arguments for tm_borders(), they are:

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.






16.4.3 Data classification methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some methods of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.
tmap provides a total ten data classification methods, namely: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.
To define a data classification method, the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() will be used.

16.4.3.1 Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
The code chunk below shows a quantile data classification that used 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








In the code chunk below, equal data classification method is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the distribution of quantile data classification method are more evenly distributed than equal data classification method.


16.4.3.2 Plotting choropleth map with custome break
For all the built-in styles, the category breaks are computed internally. In order to override these defaults, the breakpoints can be set explicitly by means of the breaks argument to the tm_fill(). It is important to note that, in tmap the breaks include a minimum and maximum. As a result, in order to end up with n categories, n+1 elements must be specified in the breaks option (the values must be in increasing order).
Before we get started, it is always a good practice to get some descriptive statistics on the variable before setting the break points. Code chunk below will be used to compute and display the descriptive statistics of DEPENDENCY field.

summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


With reference to the results above, we set break point at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. In addition, we also need to include a minimum and maximum, which we set at 0 and 100. Our breaks vector is thus c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)
Now, we will plot the choropleth map by using the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

the visual variable `fill` namely 'breaks' to fill.scale = tm_scale(<HERE>).


Warning: Values have found that are higher than the highest break. They are
assigned to the highest interval












16.4.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

16.4.4.1 Using ColourBrewer palette
To change the colour, we assign the preferred colour to values argument of tm_scale_intervals() as shown in the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the choropleth map is shaded in green.
To reverse the colour shading, add a “-” prefix.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the colour scheme has been reversed.



16.4.5 Map Layouts
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohensive map. Map elements include among others the objects to be mapped, the title, the scale bar, the compass, margins and aspects ratios. Colour settings and data classification methods covered in the previous section relate to the palette and break-points are used to affect how the map looks.

16.4.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, several tm_legend() options are provided to change the placement, format and appearance of the legend.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)")










16.4.5.2 Map style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. They can be called by using tmap_style().
The code chunk below shows the classic style is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY", 
          style = "quantile", 
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")

Beside map style, tmap also also provides arguments to draw other map furniture such as compass, scale bar and grid lines.

16.4.6 Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also referred to as facet maps, are composed of many maps arrange side-by-side, and sometimes stacked vertically. Small multiple maps enable the visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways:

by assigning multiple values to at least one of the asthetic arguments,
by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets(), and
by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange().


16.4.6.1 By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by defining ncols in tm_fill().

  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal", 
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")

title: 17 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text: Proportional symbol maps (also known as graduate symbol maps) are a class of maps that use the visual variable of size to represent differences in the magnitude of a discrete, abruptly changing phenomenon, e.g. counts of people. Like choropleth maps, you can create classed or unclassed versions of these maps. The classed ones are known as range-graded or graduated symbols, and the unclassed are called proportional symbols, where the area of the symbols are proportional to the values of the attribute being mapped. In this hands-on exercise, you will learn how to create a proportional symbol map showing the number of wins by Singapore Pools’ outlets using an R package called tmap.

text:
17.2 Learning outcome
By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will acquire the following skills by using appropriate R packages:

To import an aspatial data file into R.
To convert it into simple point feature data frame and at the same time, to assign an appropriate projection reference to the newly create simple point feature data frame.
To plot interactive proportional symbol maps.

title: 17 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
17.3 Getting Started
Before we get started, we need to ensure that tmap package of R and other related R packages have been installed and loaded into R.

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

title: 17 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
17.4 Geospatial Data Wrangling

17.4.1 The data
The data set use for this hands-on exercise is called SGPools_svy21. The data is in csv file format.
It consists of seven columns. The XCOORD and YCOORD columns are the x-coordinates and y-coordinates of SingPools outlets and branches. They are in Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinates System.


17.4.2 Data Import and Preparation
The code chunk below uses read_csv() function of readr package to import SGPools_svy21.csv into R as a tibble data frame called sgpools.

sgpools <- read_csv("data/aspatial/SGPools_svy21.csv")

17.4.3 Creating a sf data frame from an aspatial data frame
The code chunk below converts sgpools data frame into a simple feature data frame by using st_as_sf() of sf packages.

sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,

title: 17 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
17.5 Drawing Proportional Symbol Map
To create an interactive proportional symbol map in R, the view mode of tmap will be used.
The code churn below will turn on the interactive mode of tmap.

tmap_mode("view")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`



17.5.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map
The code chunks below are used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)







17.5.2 Lets make it proportional
To draw a proportional symbol map, we need to assign a numerical variable to the size visual attribute. The code chunks below show that the variable Gp1Gp2Winnings is assigned to size visual attribute.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)








17.5.3 Lets give it a different colour
The proportional symbol map can be further improved by using the colour visual attribute. In the code chunks below, OUTLET_TYPE variable is used as the colour attribute variable.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)









17.5.4 I have a twin brothers :)
An impressive and little-know feature of tmap’s view mode is that it also works with faceted plots. The argument sync in tm_facets() can be used in this case to produce multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan settings.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) + 
  tm_facets(by= "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)






















Tip




When move/zoom in/zoom out one side, the other side changes as well.
There are three map types (Esri.WorldGrayCanvas, OpenStreetMap and Esri.WorldTopoMap).



Before you end the session, it is wiser to switch tmap’s Viewer back to plot mode by using the code chunk below.

tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"

title: 18 Analytical Mapping
text:
18.4 Choropleth Map for Rates
In much of our readings we have now seen the importance to map rates rather than counts of things, and that is for the simple reason that water points are not equally distributed in space. That means that if we do not account for how many water points are somewhere, we end up mapping total water point size rather than our topic of interest.

18.4.1 Deriving Proportion of Functional Water Points and Non-Functional Water Points
We will tabulate the proportion of functional water points and the proportion of non-functional water points in each LGA. In the following code chunk, mutate() from dplyr package is used to derive two fields, namely pct_functional and pct_nonfunctional.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional/total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional/total_wp)



18.4.2 Plotting map of rate

tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons("pct_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) + 
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Rate map of functional water point by LGAs")

title: 18 Analytical Mapping
text:
18.5 Extreme Value Maps
Extreme value maps are variations of common choropleth maps where the classification is designed to highlight extreme values at the lower and upper end of the scale, with the goal of identifying outliers. These maps were developed in the spirit of spatializing EDA, i.e., adding spatial features to commonly used approaches in non-spatial EDA (Anselin 1994).

18.5.1 Percentile Map
The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0-1%,1-10%, 10-50%,50-90%,90-99%, and 99-100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be derived by means of the base R quantile command, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1). Note that the begin and endpoint need to be included.

18.5.1.1 Data Preparation
Step 1: Exclude records with NA by using the code chunk below.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()

Step 2: Creating customised classification and extracting values

percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[,1], percent)

       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








Important



When variables are extracted from an sf data.frame, the geometry is extracted as well. For mapping and spatial manipulation, this is the expected behavior, but many base R functions cannot deal with the geometry. Specifically, the quantile() gives an error. As a result st_set_geomtry(NULL) is used to drop geomtry field.




18.5.1.2 Why writing functions?
Writing a function has three big advantages over using copy-and-paste:

You can give a function an evocative name that makes your code easier to understand.
As requirements change, you only need to update code in one place, instead of many.
You eliminate the chance of making incidental mistakes when you copy and paste (i.e. updating a variable name in one place, but not in another).

Source: Chapter 19: Functions of R for Data Science.


18.5.1.3 Creating the get.var function
Firstly, we will write an R function as shown below to extract a variable (i.e. wp_nonfunctional) as a vector out of an sf data.frame.

arguments:

vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of sf data frame

returns:

v: vector with values (without a column name)



get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% 
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}



18.5.1.4 A percentile mapping function
Next, we will write a percentile mapping function by using the code chunk below.

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle=NA, mtitle="Percentile Map"){
  percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(vnam,
                title=legtitle,
                breaks=bperc,
                palette="Blues",
                labels=c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%", "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%"))  +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle, 
              title.position = c("right","bottom"))
}



18.5.1.5 Test drive the percentile mapping function
To run the function, type the code chunk as shown below.

percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)

Note that this is just a bare bones implementation. Additional arguments such as the title, legend positioning just to name a few of them, could be passed to customise various features of the map.



18.5.2 Box map
In essence, a box map is an augmented quartile map, with an additional lower and upper category. When there are lower outliers, then the starting point for the breaks is the minimum value, and the second break is the lower fence. In contrast, when there are no lower outliers, then the starting point for the breaks will be the lower fence, and the second break is the minimum value (there will be no observations that fall in the interval between the lower fence and the minimum value).

ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()









Displaying summary statistics on a choropleth map by using the basic principles of boxplot.
To create a box map, a custom breaks specification will be used. However, there is a complication. The break points for the box map vary depending on whether lower or upper outliers are present.


18.5.2.1 Creating the boxbreaks function
The code chunk below is an R function that creating break points for a box map.

arguments:

v: vector with observations
mult: multiplier for IQR (default 1.5)

returns:

bb: vector with 7 break points compute quartile and fences



boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}



18.5.2.2 Creating the get.var function
The code chunk below is an R function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame.

arguments:

vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of sf data frame

returns:

v: vector with values (without a column name)



get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}



18.5.2.3 Test drive the newly created function
Let’s test the newly created function

var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp) 
boxbreaks(var)

[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




18.5.2.4 Boxmap function
The code chunk below is an R function to create a box map. - arguments: - vnam: variable name (as character, in quotes) - df: simple features polygon layer - legtitle: legend title - mtitle: map title - mult: multiplier for IQR - returns: - a tmap-element (plots a map).

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,title=legtitle,
            breaks=bb,
            palette="Blues",
            labels = c("lower outlier", 
                       "< 25%", 
                       "25% - 50%", 
                       "50% - 75%",
                       "> 75%", 
                       "upper outlier"))  +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle, 
              title.position = c("left",
                                 "top"))
}


tmap_mode("plot")

ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`
